analysis.one_liner: Forces annual offshore oil and gas lease sales in the Gulf of Mexico and Alaska.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Natural Resources Committee without a vote; it was referred to a subcommittee in February 2023 and no action was ever taken on it.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the Interior Department to hold at least two offshore oil and gas lease sales every year in the Gulf of Mexico and at least two in Alaska's federal waters, and to offer up all unleased acreage in each sale. It would also have barred the President from pausing or canceling offshore oil and gas leasing without approval from Congress, with a presumption that any such pause is illegal. It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its energy subcommittee, and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies that want guaranteed access to federal offshore waters. The bill would lock in a minimum number of lease sales each year in the Gulf of Mexico and Alaska regardless of market demand or an administration's energy policy, and would make it much harder for any President to slow or stop offshore drilling without Congress agreeing.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Interior Department to hold at least two region-wide lease sales annually in each of the Central and Western Gulf of Mexico planning areas, starting in fiscal 2023.
Requires at least two region-wide lease sales annually in the Alaska region of the Outer Continental Shelf.
Requires each sale to include all unleased areas not subject to existing restrictions, opening maximum acreage to bidding.

Amends the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to prohibit the President from unreasonably pausing, canceling, or delaying federal offshore oil and gas leasing without congressional approval, with a rebuttable presumption that any such action without approval is unreasonable.

analysis.who_pays: The public, which owns the offshore lands being leased. Mandated annual drilling in the Gulf of Mexico and Alaska would add emissions and spill risk to coastal communities, fishing grounds, and Alaska Native subsistence areas, and would remove a President's ability to adjust leasing policy without a vote of Congress. Alaska lease sales in recent years have drawn little or no bidder interest, so forcing them offers little revenue and much downside.

drawbacks.text: The bill ties the government's hands: lease sales would be mandatory every year regardless of market demand, environmental review, or which party controls the White House.
It strips the President of authority to pause or delay offshore leasing without congressional approval, and presumes any such pause is unreasonable — a one-way rule in favor of drilling.
Supporters' own framing (guaranteed sales, maximum acreage) concedes the bill prioritizes leasing volume over whether drilling makes sense in sensitive waters off Alaska and the Gulf.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains flow almost entirely to one industry: guaranteed annual access to federal offshore acreage and protection from presidential action. The costs — climate emissions, spill risk, and the loss of flexibility for future administrations — are diffuse and borne by the public. There is no counterweight in the bill for conservation, coastal protection, or revenue to the Treasury.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Natural Resources Committee and its energy subcommittee for the entire two-year Congress and never received a markup or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Jerry L. Carl (R-AL) introduced the bill on January 13, 2023, with 13 original cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Committee on Natural Resources the same day.
On February 21, 2023, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, and the action record shows no further action for the rest of the Congress.
Seventeen House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
The 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025, and the bill expired without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public's coastal and environmental interests, and any future administration wanting flexibility over offshore leasing — the mandate never took effect. Oil and gas companies lost a guaranteed annual pipeline of federal offshore leases, though it cost them nothing since they never had it.

for.name: Jerry L. Carl
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 13 original cosponsors.

for.name: 17 of 224 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all recorded support was Republican.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee / Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action after the February 21, 2023 subcommittee referral; the bill was never reported or scheduled for a floor vote.

against.name: Biden administration
against.what_they_did: The administration the bill targeted had moved to limit new offshore leasing, proposing a five-year Outer Continental Shelf program with no new lease sales; the bill would have overridden that approach.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 17 cosponsors were House Republicans, and there is no record of any Democratic support; the bill never reached a vote where the split could be measured.

industries.note: The bill guarantees producers two mandatory lease sales a year in the Gulf of Mexico and two in Alaska, with maximum acreage offered, and shields leasing from presidential action. The cost — emissions, spill risk to fisheries and coastlines — lands on the public that owns these waters.
Mandated annual sales create a guaranteed pipeline of offshore drilling work regardless of demand, at public environmental expense.

industries.industry: Gulf and Alaska coastal fishing and tourism
industries.note: Expanded offshore leasing raises spill risk in the waters these industries depend on; the bill offers them nothing in return.
